video_title: The Market Creates Its Own Trends — Richard Brennan | Systematic Investor | Ep.418
gist: METADATA MISMATCH: the title/channel record (Top Traders Unplugged, Richard Brennan) does not match the actual transcript, which is a Pompliano-style interview with macro/AI-crypto strategist Jordy Visser (Vise Labs / AI22V Research). Visser argues the classic liquidity cycle is broken by AI-driven productivity, that crypto rails are 'ghost cities' about to be lit up by AI agents (not humans) as the real users, and that Bitcoin is his only 30-year-conviction asset while altcoins like Zcash/Near/Instinct AI are the higher-beta bet on agent-driven commerce.

themes.theme: The Liquidity Cycle Is Broken by AI Productivity

insights.claim: Since June 30, 2025 (end of Q2), the Nasdaq and S&P 500 are roughly flat while oil and 10-year yields have risen sharply and Bitcoin/Ethereum/AI stocks have still climbed, undercutting the assumption that higher rates and oil must crash risk assets.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should stop pricing 'higher rates/oil = risk-off' as a reliable mechanical trade in the current regime.
insights.quote: Stocks are unchanged, both NASDAQ and S&P. Oil's a lot higher... Tenure rates, they're up a lot.

insights.claim: Visser argues the U.S. no longer experiences prolonged recessions because policymakers treat sustained stock-market declines as unacceptable and will deploy a 'monetary bazooka' whenever needed, and he personally does not expect to see an 18-month recession again in his lifetime.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Implies dip-buying on recession fear has structurally higher odds of being rewarded than historical base rates suggest.
insights.quote: I don't think I'll see that again in my lifetime.

insights.claim: Non-healthcare hiring has been negative for roughly the last 20 months even as S&P 500 earnings grew near 30%, evidence that corporate profit growth has decoupled from job creation for the first time in this cycle.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Payrolls/GDP are becoming lagging or misleading signals for equity investors; earnings and margins matter more than headline jobs data.
insights.quote: We've had no job creation over the last 20 months except for healthcare.

insights.claim: The traditional liquidity mechanism (M2 growth -> GDP -> job creation) is broken; instead, liquidity is converting directly into corporate profit margins and topline revenue rather than employment, which is why equities keep rising despite weak hiring.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Investors using classic M2/GDP liquidity-cycle models to time markets are working from a broken model, per Visser.
insights.quote: We have broken the liquidity mechanism.

insights.claim: Visser predicts the next major source of system liquidity will be tokenization unlocking an estimated $900 trillion of largely dormant assets (about two-thirds of which currently sit idle) as programmable collateral, rather than any Fed/M2-based liquidity measure.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Points to tokenized RWA/collateral platforms as a structurally underappreciated liquidity source for the next cycle.
insights.quote: Tokenization unleashes dormant assets $900 trillion of assets of which two thirds just sit and do nothing.

insights.claim: There has been a roughly 18-month divergence between rising M2 money supply and a lagging Bitcoin price (the 'alligator jaws'); the Bitcoin community expects a violent catch-up move, but Visser argues this M2-driven framework is now outdated because Bitcoin's price will increasingly be driven by real AI-agent usage rather than by liquidity alone.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Warns Bitcoin holders against relying purely on the M2-catchup thesis; usage-driven demand is the framework he'd actually trade on.
insights.quote: There have been times where they diverged and you get kind of the alligator... mouth, but then when it closes, there's a violent move in Bitcoin to catch up to M2.

insights.claim: Visser argues 2020's lockdown-yet-stocks-finished-higher episode permanently broke investor psychology, conditioning market participants to keep buying regardless of bad news — a structural, self-reinforcing support for equities beyond any single macro driver.
insights.speaker: Host (interviewer)
insights.so_what: Explains persistent 'buy the dip' resilience as a behavioral/psychological regime shift, not just liquidity.
insights.quote: It just was like we pulled back the curtain like Wizard of Oz style and everyone's like, 'Wait a minute. No matter what happens, if you keep buying stocks, you're going to make money.'

insights.claim: Visser lists a chain of feared catalysts since 2019 (COVID lockdowns, 2022's fastest-ever Fed rate hikes with double-digit inflation, SVB's collapse, 2025 tariffs, and a Strait of Hormuz conflict) that all failed to produce a sustained recession, arguing markets are far less sensitive to conventional macro shocks than commentators assume.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A track record of failed recession calls argues for discounting recurring 'this time the shock will break the market' narratives.
insights.quote: So, Smoot Holy, straight of Hormuz, bank runs, a pandemic, and the most aggressive Fed rate hikes in history, no recessions.

themes.theme: Outdated Economic Metrics in an Agent Economy

insights.claim: Visser's own company operates with fewer than 15 human employees but roughly 100 AI/digital agent 'employees,' illustrating that value creation is shifting to non-human agents in ways GDP and payroll statistics do not capture.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, first-person data point that headcount-based productivity/labor metrics understate real output in AI-native firms.
insights.quote: There are less than 15 humans that work there. We may have close to 100 digital AI agent employees.

insights.claim: Visser argues investors who keep anchoring investment decisions to legacy macro metrics (GDP, payrolls) will structurally underperform because those metrics are miscalibrated for an economy where AI agents, not humans, are driving marginal output.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Direct call to re-weight investment process away from traditional macro dashboards toward AI-adoption/usage signals.
insights.quote: If you keep looking at those metrics trying to invest in the future, you're going to struggle.

insights.claim: Higher oil and rates are hitting 'old economy' segments (homebuilders, consumer staples) but not moving the earnings of AI-exposed names like Micron or Google, creating a bifurcated market where headline macro sensitivity masks divergent underlying exposure.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Sector selection (AI-exposed vs. rate/oil-exposed) matters more right now than a single macro call on rates or oil.
insights.quote: It doesn't change Micron's earnings. It doesn't change Google's earnings.

insights.claim: The AIQ AI-focused ETF is up roughly 25% year-to-date as of the recording, evidence that AI-exposed equities have decoupled from the rate/oil-sensitive parts of the market.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A quantifiable benchmark for how far AI-thematic equities are outrunning the broader index amid macro headwinds.
insights.quote: AIQ, the AI ETF is up, I think I looked this morning, 25% year-to-date.

themes.theme: AI Agent Capability Leap and Safety Overhang

insights.claim: OpenAI reportedly used roughly 10,000 collaborating AI agents to solve the Navier-Stokes problem (a Fields-Medal-caliber math problem), demonstrating that agent collaboration at scale, not just raw model intelligence, is now unlocking previously unsolved problems.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Signals a step-change in AI's applied research capability that could accelerate breakthroughs across math, physics, and biotech.
insights.quote: They had 10,000 agents deal with the problem.

insights.claim: Visser's framework: many hard human research problems reach the '20-yard line' via siloed individual effort but stall because human collaboration doesn't scale or 'go viral'; swarms of AI agents can now finish that last mile, citing Eli Lilly using agents to mine dormant, previously-funded biotech research and IP toward cures (e.g., cancer, cholesterol).
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Points to dormant biotech IP as an underappreciated asset class that AI-agent-driven R&D could suddenly reprice.
insights.quote: All of this dormant IP that exists, all these biotech companies, they've got something that people invested in... let's finish it.

insights.claim: Andrew Yang stated publicly (on CNBC) that an AI lab leader told him agents can self-replicate code and have already littered the internet, and that Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly building a 'synthetic internet' to train future models on cleaner data. Visser estimates roughly a 20% probability this specific claim is true.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A low-probability but high-impact tail risk/catalyst investors in AI infrastructure and safety-adjacent names should be aware of, even if unconfirmed.
insights.quote: This sounds batshit crazy, but given the times we're living in, it's not a 0% probability. Like, I don't know, maybe it's a 20% probability that's what happened.

insights.claim: Visser argues the recent OpenAI/Anthropic safety 'pause' tied to self-replication concerns is likely an overreaction that will not slow compute buildout and may even accelerate compute investment, based on direct outreach he received from hedge funds ahead of the Monday market open.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A contrarian near-term read that AI safety scares tend to be buying opportunities for compute/AI infrastructure exposure, not selling signals.
insights.quote: This will not stop compute. If anything, it'll probably accelerate compute.

insights.claim: Negative AI narratives (e.g., a Matt Schumer article on job losses getting 170 million views) get vastly more public attention than positive AI breakthroughs (e.g., cancer vaccines), which Visser argues causes markets and the public to systematically misprice AI's net effect as more negative than warranted.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests fading headline-driven AI doom narratives and instead tracking underlying earnings/usage data for a more accurate read.
insights.quote: Nobody wants to hear about the good news that's coming from AI. They only want to hear about the bad news.

insights.claim: Despite his overall AI bullishness, Visser says he is not bullish on public equity market growth by 2030, citing Leopold Aschenbrenner's 'Situational Awareness' timeline (AI progress tracking on-pace or ~6 months ahead of that forecast) and warning that societal/political disruption (e.g., political polarization over data centers) could cap public-market equity upside even as the underlying technology keeps advancing.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A notably bearish carve-out from an otherwise AI-bull: public equity index returns may lag the technology's progress due to political/social friction.
insights.quote: I am not bullish on the growth in public equities as an investment by the time we get to 2030.

themes.theme: Crypto as 'Ghost Rails' Waiting for AI Agent Users

insights.claim: Visser's central thesis: crypto/blockchain infrastructure has been overbuilt ahead of demand, like China's empty 'ghost cities' — dormant until real users arrive; he argues that moment is now, with AI agents (not humans) becoming the transacting users that finally light up these rails.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes crypto valuation from 'human adoption' metrics to 'agent transaction volume' as the key leading indicator to track.
insights.quote: That's where crypto is right now. They're ghost rails... That's why the swarm equals crypto guardrails.

insights.claim: Visser argues blockchain is structurally necessary for agent-to-agent commerce because it provides trustless, near-instant settlement and (via privacy-focused chains) anonymity for machine-to-machine transactions, replacing legacy finance intermediaries who profit from slow settlement.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Provides a fundamental (non-speculative) demand driver for blockchain settlement and privacy-chain infrastructure tied to agent commerce.
insights.quote: Agents will be transacting with each other. The blockchain is necessary.

insights.claim: Visser flags Zcash and Near Protocol rallying specifically in September as leading indicators of real agent-driven privacy and agent-to-agent transaction demand, distinguishing this from generic 'DeFi' speculation narratives.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Gives investors specific tickers to watch as proxies for the agent-commerce thesis rather than broad crypto beta.
insights.quote: I'm watching Zcash and Near because they represent the... agentic stuff is picking up every day.

insights.claim: Tether is cited as investing hundreds of millions of dollars into AI; Visser interprets this as CEO-level (Paolo Ardoino) positioning to combine AI models, privacy agents, and stablecoins into one integrated stack.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: An underappreciated corporate-strategy signal: the largest stablecoin issuer is building AI capability, not just holding reserves.
insights.quote: Why is Tether investing so much money in AI? My belief is because Paolo understands exactly what's happening.

insights.claim: Stripe's Tempo stablecoin chart shows a sharp adoption ramp; Visser draws a comparison to Figure Technologies deliberately seeding both sides of a two-sided market (starting with loan origination) to bootstrap a new clearing/settlement network, suggesting Stripe could be doing something similar to jump-start Tempo.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Raises the possibility that Tempo's adoption curve is partly engineered/seeded, worth diligence before treating it as pure organic demand.
insights.quote: Is Stripe somehow pushing it and giving it an advantage? Is there some sort of like seeding?

insights.claim: Robinhood Chain's early transaction activity was mostly meme-token driven; Visser frames meme speculation as a normal precursor phase that shows up on a new rail before genuine agent-driven transaction volume arrives.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Meme activity on a new chain shouldn't be dismissed as noise — it can be an early-stage signal preceding real usage.
insights.quote: Robin Hood chain was mainly meme stuff... you have meme activity before everyone else gets on board, before the agents start transacting.

insights.claim: Applying a Peter Thiel heuristic ('the steeper the valuation climb, the more likely the company is undervalued'), Visser cites Instinct AI going from roughly a $500 million to $2.5 billion to $10 billion valuation in under three months, on an 80% gross-margin (pre-COGS) business.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable private-market valuation data point supporting the personal-assistant-agent investment thesis.
insights.quote: The more steep the valuation climb, the more likely the company's undervalued.

insights.claim: Regulators reportedly granted a roughly 5-year exemption enabling broad tokenization of real-world assets to proceed, which Visser calls a bigger deal than the Clarity Act and the single most important step in unlocking dormant collateral/liquidity into the financial system.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Flags a specific regulatory catalyst investors should track as more consequential than the more widely-discussed Clarity Act.
insights.quote: If you ask me what's more important than stable coins, tokenizing things is the most important step we're taking in this entire crypto place.

themes.theme: Bitcoin's Role vs. Altcoins: A 30-Year Conviction Asset

insights.claim: Visser states Bitcoin is the only asset he holds high conviction will keep rising in value over a 30-year horizon (not just 3-5 years), positioning other crypto assets as higher-risk 'innovation' bets subject to competitive catch-up and shrinking terminal value.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A clear long-horizon portfolio anchor: Bitcoin as the core holding, altcoins as tactical/speculative satellite positions.
insights.quote: I want an asset that will be growing in value for the next 30 years... that I believe is Bitcoin. That's it.

insights.claim: Visser maps crypto adoption onto the internet's historical timeline: Netscape's 1994 IPO to the 2007 iPhone to the 2009 App Store spanned ~14-15 years; he argues Bitcoin (whitepaper ~2008/2009) is on the same ~15-year timeline now reaching its 'smartphone moment,' with AI agents serving as the killer-app users that finally drive adoption.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Offers a historical analog for timing crypto's mainstream adoption inflection point around AI agents rather than human retail adoption.
insights.quote: Netscape was 94. The iPhone was 2007. It was 13 years... We're on the exact same timeline.

insights.claim: Visser's explicit trading marker for his agent-adoption thesis: if Bitcoin were below $80,000 by the end of October, he would consider that a problem for the thesis; during the recording, Bitcoin traded back above $80,000, which he treats as thesis-confirming in real time.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, falsifiable price level and date investors can use to test Visser's own thesis going forward.
insights.quote: If Bitcoin is below 80,000, okay, I'll even say by the end of October, there's a problem.

insights.claim: Visser identifies roughly $82,000 as a key high-volume breakout/capitulation level from the post-October-10 selloff; per his Micron-trade playbook, once Bitcoin decisively reclaims and holds above such a level amid rising agent activity, it 'should not look back' — but he notes that decisive breakout had not yet occurred as of the interview.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Provides a specific technical level tying his fundamental agent-adoption thesis to an actionable price trigger.
insights.quote: When we get above 82,000... that's the point in time when I think people gave up the last time.

insights.claim: Visser distinguishes Bitcoin and Ethereum's role (trusted, large-transaction collateral that makes institutions comfortable) from smaller/newer chains, which need genuine entrepreneurial and now agent-driven activity to justify their valuations; he personally did not buy Bitcoin early but bought into 'the blockchain' thesis in 2014-15 after visiting Silicon Valley and Singularity University in 2013.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Explains his portfolio construction logic: BTC/ETH as the trusted collateral base layer, altcoins as the innovation/entrepreneurial layer.
insights.quote: I did buy into by 2014 and 15 into the blockchain. It made sense to me that this is where business would be conducted.

insights.claim: Visser warns crypto bulls against assuming Bitcoin needs a generational wealth transfer from aging baby boomers to reach a hypothetical $20 trillion market cap — a multi-decade dependent path — versus real usage-driven demand from AI agents, which he argues could get there faster.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes the bull case for Bitcoin's ultimate market cap away from a slow demographic wealth-transfer story toward a faster usage-driven one.
insights.quote: If you think that Bitcoin was going to get to 20 trillion without the wealthy old baby boomers to believe in it, you're crazy.

insights.claim: The host states he believes Sylvia (Vise/Visser's publicly traded vehicle) is the only publicly traded company explicitly merging AI and Bitcoin exposure together, and Visser agrees.
insights.speaker: Host (interviewer)
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, narrow public-equity vehicle positioned at the intersection of the episode's two core themes (AI and Bitcoin).
insights.quote: I am pretty sure that Sylvia in the public markets is the only publicly traded company that is merging AI and Bitcoin together.

themes.theme: The Personal AI Assistant / Agent Commerce Economy

insights.claim: Visser describes Instinct AI autonomously rebooking a breakfast reservation and calendar invite (moving it from Thursday to Friday) without being given payment/account credentials, illustrating agents handling multi-step real-world logistics end-to-end.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of agent reliability for real scheduling/logistics tasks, supporting the personal-assistant investment thesis.
insights.quote: I just said, move the reservation to Friday. And it instinctively knew move the calendar invite, cancel Thursday, make reservation for Friday.

insights.claim: Instinct AI is rolling out a wallet feature capped at $100 (a programmable spending limit, likened to a Dunkin' Donuts gift card) so users can safely delegate small purchases (Uber, DoorDash, Amazon) to their agent without runaway-spend risk.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Programmable spend caps are the product mechanism that will actually enable consumer-agent commerce to scale safely — worth watching as a template other agent platforms will copy.
insights.quote: It has a maximum because it's programmable. You can't do more than this.

insights.claim: Visser argues the most underrated layer in the AI agent stack is shared memory/context — not the underlying model or the interface — because without persistent shared memory across apps, users resist switching between competing personal assistants (Instinct, Grok, Meta's Muse) each time a new one launches.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Investors should look for who owns/controls the persistent memory layer across agents as a potential moat, rather than focusing purely on model quality.
insights.quote: I am shocked at how little attention the memory layer is getting.

insights.claim: A secondhand, unverified anecdote suggests AI pricing agents on airline sites (e.g., Delta) may dynamically raise prices for the same user across repeat visits by inferring willingness-to-pay, potentially foreshadowing 'agent vs. agent' commerce where buyer-side agents counter with anonymized shopping to defeat seller-side price discrimination.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: If true, this dynamic creates structural demand for privacy/anonymity tools (e.g., privacy-focused blockchains) to let buyer-agents avoid seller-agent price discrimination.
insights.quote: The agents are driving the price higher thinking that... they're trying to personalize the ability of the person to pay.

insights.claim: Visser predicts consumer agent-driven commerce and payments will be 'the story for the next year,' with AI agents becoming the actual transacting users of blockchain rails rather than humans.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Sets a specific near-term (12-month) thematic bet: watch agent-driven transaction/payment volume as the next major crypto/AI catalyst.
insights.quote: They're about to suck up transactions and payments because consumer agents will be the story for the next year.

insights.claim: Meta's stock rebounded from 52-week lows to back above its 200-day moving average following the launch of its Muse personal-assistant product, which Visser links to Zuckerberg's earlier internal admission (a leaked town hall roughly three months prior) of being disappointed in Meta's AI progress.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Ties a specific corporate product launch directly to a stock-price technical recovery, useful as a case study for how agent-product news moves large-cap tech equities.
insights.quote: Meta's stock was trading near 52-week lows. Now it's back above the 200 day moving average.

insights.claim: Visser is building a new thematic framework/index around which public companies benefit from AI agents: the Mag7, Salesforce (agents extend the value of its CRM installed base within Fortune 500 companies), and cybersecurity stocks (agents both create new attack surface and must defend against it).
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete stock-selection framework: look beyond pure AI infrastructure to software/security names whose value proposition is strengthened by agent proliferation.
insights.quote: If you believe agents are here, well then cyber is worth more because they can disrupt anything... Salesforce actually does have usefulness at this point.

insights.claim: Anthropic and OpenAI could together control as much as a third to 50% of global AI compute within a year (per comments Brad Gerstner made publicly at a summit/on a podcast), which Visser says is functionally 'the AI bubble' since compute is today's equivalent of the entire S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Flags extreme compute concentration risk in two private companies as the real locus of 'AI bubble' concern, more than public AI-linked equities.
insights.quote: They're going to control as much as 50% of compute a year from now... Compute is the entire S&P 500 right now as far as I'm concerned.

themes.theme: Trading Playbook: The Micron/Inference Case Study

insights.claim: Visser built his Micron/inference thesis by publishing analysis in May 2025 (citing Sundar Pichai's disclosed token-usage figures and roughly 20 earnings reports showing an 'inference explosion'), yet institutional buying did not arrive until October — a multi-month lag between public data availability and institutional recognition that he says left investors 'no excuse' for missing the trade at $110.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a repeatable pattern: publicly available fundamental data can precede institutional recognition by 4-6 months, creating an exploitable window for early movers.
insights.quote: You have no excuses as an investor to not have bought Micron at 110.

insights.claim: Visser's explicit playbook for early-stage themes: enter very early before consensus forms, then treat a decisive break above key resistance/volume levels as confirmation that the trend should not reverse — he states crypto/Bitcoin had not yet delivered that decisive breakout confirmation as of the interview.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A transferable technical-plus-fundamental framework for timing entries in emerging themes (get in early, then wait for a technical confirmation signal before sizing up).
insights.quote: Once it starts breaking above key levels, it should not look back. We haven't done that yet in Bitcoin and the ecosystem.
